36.name: Cwen
36.province: the head of the southern gulf
36.history: Cwen is the larger of the landings on the southern gulf, a wide bay of quiet water where the fish come in on the tide in shoals. Its households fished with nets of twisted fibre and sank them with beach stones, and it was a net-maker of Cwen who began the long mesh, a net long enough to close across the bay's inner arm, and set it there with the help of every household on the shore. Households came from along the coast to see the closed net. Her weights were notched with three strokes each, cut with a hard stone into the soft beach pebble, so that a weight knew its own net; her daughter learned the groove, spoiled her first stones, and cut the three strokes true before her mother's eyes failed. The daughter took up a way of holding each finished weight a breath longer in the light than the work required, as though the three strokes were worth looking at for their own sake. Every weight of the Cwen nets was notched the same way after, and the three strokes are the eldest mark on the island made again and again of purpose. At the close of the age some hundred and fifty souls live at Cwen, the largest landing of the south coast, and the notched weights lie thick on the floor of the bay where the nets have torn.
36.known_for: the net-weights notched with three strokes, the eldest mark on the island

14.name: Cwen
14.history: The southern Cwen is a small landing on the southern shore, its boats drawn up on flat stones at the head of a sandy cove. For most of the age its midden grew slowly, a household's meals at a time. Then, once the heights were left, whole kin-groups came down from the abandoned rings and the lands about them, and some settled here; the midden began to grow as fast as the mound at the eastern Dunn had grown when it was young, and in the end outgrew it. A landing once counted by the dozen was counted by the score. The people of the landings raised no new work anywhere out of sight of salt water after that time, and the southern Cwen is the place where the turning is plainest to see. At the close of the age it holds some two hundred souls, more than any landing of the south but its namesake on the gulf, and a new row of houses stands behind the old.
14.known_for: the midden that outgrew the eastern Dunn

139.name: Cwen
139.province: the southern coast, east of the southern Cwen
139.history: The third Cwen is a small landing a short way along the southern coast from the second, on a harbour sheltered by a reef that breaks the swell at half tide. Its households came to it from the southern Cwen in the lifetimes when the holy woods of the east were first set aside by the hill-folk, and they carried the name with them as a household carries its fire, so that the south coast had two Cwens within a morning's rowing of each other. They fished the reef and took shellfish from the pools inside it, and hunted seal on the skerries when the seals came. After the heights were left and the south coast filled with households come down to the shore, this Cwen grew with its neighbour; its landing stones were relaid and lengthened, and a second row of houses raised behind the first. At the close of the age some sixty souls live there.
139.known_for: its reef-sheltered landing on the south coast

295.name: Dunn
295.history: The southern Dunn is a landing on the southern coast at the head of a beach of fine sand, where the swell runs long and the whales go by in their seasons. A whale stranded below it one autumn, and the households of the whole shore came to cut it and share it out; its oil was kept in bladders and clay pots and burned in stone lamps through two winters at least, and its ribs were driven upright into the ground for the frames of three round houses roofed with turf. The first rib cracked through within a few years, and the houses were raised a second time on the sound bone; a child digging by the wall turned up the buried foot of the first rib and the landing kept it by the door. A third raising stood on bone carried along the shore from a whale cut further west, word of usable ribs travelling faster by then than word of strandings once had. The landing also has a short mole of heaped stone at the western end of the beach, where the boats lie in the worst weather. At the close of the age some ninety souls live there, in houses framed on whale-bone and on timber both.

465.name: Morn
465.province: the southern coast, on the oyster headland
465.history: The southern Morn lies on a low headland of the southern coast where the oyster beds are close enough inshore to be raked from the rocks at low water, and it has little else. Its households raked oyster, whelk and cockle and heaped the shells over the whole headland, until the mound stood taller than any household's reach and the houses were built on the shell itself. A worn rake was laid on the mound by the household that had used it longest when its owner died. The raking households found that the oysters of the lowest layers of their mound were broader by half than any taken from the same water in living memory, and did not trouble over why; the beds were raked every summer and never rested. At the close of the age the landing holds some forty souls, and the white of the headland can be seen from far out to sea, whiter than any cliff on that coast.
465.known_for: its headland of heaped shell and the great oysters at the bottom of the heap

110.name: Bral
110.history: The eastern Bral is a landing on the south-eastern coast with a line of fish-kilns above its beach like those of Morn, within a day's rowing along the coast. The woman who minded the middle kiln judged the smoke by its smell at first light and dusk and the fish by the give of the flesh under one finger, and taught both by standing a child at her elbow; a girl of the landing learned to read the smoke well enough to tell a kiln going wrong from the far end of the beach. The kilns were kept alight in relay by the households in the busy weeks, one household taking the night and another the day. When a whale stranded on the beach, the landing gave dried fish to the southern landings for a share of its oil, and the two kept up the giving for a generation. At the close of the age the landing holds some hundred souls, and the smell of its kilns reaches the grazing above the shore in any wind off the sea.
110.known_for: its line of fish-kilns in the south-east

94.name: Vell
94.province: the south-eastern coast, opposite Eilean dhearg
94.history: The eastern Vell lies on the south-eastern coast facing Eilean dhearg across a short sound. Its households built round houses of dry stone, each with a hearth sunk in the middle of the floor and, beneath that, a drain running out under the wall; the first house was raised on a knoll above the landing, and the first drain cut beneath a wall came after the floor had stood wet through a winter. Households whose houses were built without a drain took up their floors in a dry season and cut the channel in under walls already standing, having watched their neighbours' floors stand drier. Fourteen houses were finished in the end. The dead of the Vell were rowed across the sound to Eilean dhearg and laid in stone boxes facing the mainland, and no box was left standing open through a night: an unfinished one was covered with brush and stone until its lid could be rowed across. Forty boxes are counted on the island. At the close of the age some hundred souls live in the house-rings, and the boats that carry the dead still go out from the same stone.
94.known_for: its round houses with sunk hearths and drains, and its dead on Eilean dhearg

128.name: Warr
128.province: the southern shore of the gulf
128.history: The eastern Warr is a small landing on the southern shore of the gulf, across the water from the eastern Bral and in sight of its kiln smoke. Its households were fishers and weed-gatherers who came to it from the west of the gulf in the lifetimes when the long house was built into the cliff at the north-eastern Tarr, and they carried with them the name of the shell-road landing on Loch chrom, though no road was ever made here. They fish the quiet water inside the gulf and dry their catch on racks rather than in kilns, and trade what they dry across the water. At the close of the age it is a landing of some thirty souls, content with the gulf's shelter, whose boats go out in weather that keeps the open-sea landings ashore.
128.known_for: its sheltered landing on the gulf

313.name: Toll
313.province: the Abhainn uaine, in the midlands
313.history: The midland Toll is a landing of Seann-Dhaoine inland, on the Abhainn uaine, where a shelf of rock runs out into the river and the water pools behind it. Its households cut a channel through the shelf into a pool beside the river, with slots at the channel's mouth for a wattle gate; when the river fell the gate was dropped and the pool emptied by hand, and the fish left stranded in it were taken with baskets. A boy of the landing lost two fingers to the mallet in the cutting of the slots. A child of the landing learned the floor of the channel by her feet at low water, which stretch stood firm and which gave, long before she had a word for it. In a summer when the river fell low and stayed low the gate was dropped three times before the autumn rains, and the households reckoned the late summer by the droppings. A woman of Toll walked the coast once as far as the cut cliff at Tarr, and came home saying the signs were there and no more. At the close of the age some sixty souls live at the landing, one of the two landings of Seann-Dhaoine a day's walk from salt water that were not left when the heights were, since their rivers run to the sea.
313.known_for: the fish-channel and the gate-slot cut in the rock

162.name: Vell
162.province: the Abhainn fhionn, above the lake country
162.history: The inland Vell is a landing on a river of the midlands, reached by Seann-Dhaoine' boats poling up from the coast. Its households came to it in the lifetimes when the holy woods of the east were first let alone, settling on a shelf of gravel where the river runs slow and the eels are thick, and raised a few round houses there in the manner of the coast. They lived on eels and on what the river brought, and kept their boats on the gravel. When the heights were left and every new work of Seann-Dhaoine was made by salt water, the inland Vell was not abandoned, since the river runs to the sea and the landing's boats go down it every season; but it did not grow, and its young people went down to the coast. At the close of the age it holds a few households only, some twenty souls.
162.known_for: its gravel landing on the river
